n: Now secure, David remembers his covenant with Jonathan and asks whether anyone from Saul’s family is still alive so he can show them kindness. Ancient kings often wiped out rival families; David does the opposite.
Ziba, a former servant of Saul’s household, is summoned to give information.
David speaks of showing “the kindness of God” — the generous, faithful love God shows. Ziba mentions Jonathan’s son, who is disabled in both feet.

f.g: Kindness like God’s own: undeserved, loyal, and generous.

n: Mephibosheth is living in Lo-debar, east of the Jordan, in the home of Machir — a man who later helps David too.

f.g: The name may mean “no pasture” or “nothing” — a fitting picture of his humble, hidden life.

n: David sends for him. For Saul’s grandson, a summons from the new king could have felt terrifying.
Mephibosheth falls on his face before David in fear and submission, calling himself the king’s servant.

f.g: Bowed low to show respect and submission.

n: David’s first words are “Fear not.” He restores Saul’s family land to him and invites him to eat at the royal table for the rest of his life — an honor usually reserved for the king’s own family.

f.w: eat bread at my table continually

n: Mephibosheth is overwhelmed and calls himself a “dead dog,” the lowest possible term. His humility mirrors how unworthy anyone feels before undeserved grace.

f.g: A phrase of extreme self-abasement — something worthless and contemptible.

n: David formally transfers all of Saul’s estates to Mephibosheth before Ziba as a witness.
Ziba and his large household will farm the land and supply its produce, but Mephibosheth himself will always eat with the king.

f.g: A large household, showing Ziba was a man of some wealth and influence.

n: Ziba promises to obey. David repeats that Mephibosheth will eat at his table “as one of the king’s sons.” Many readers see in this a picture of grace: the Lord welcomes the broken into His family because of a covenant made with another.

f.w: as one of the king's sons

n: Mephibosheth has a young son, Micha, so Jonathan’s line continues. Ziba’s whole household now serves him.
The chapter ends with a tender image: the disabled son of Jonathan living in Jerusalem, a permanent guest at the king’s table. His lameness is mentioned again to highlight how freely he was honored.
